For each integer \(n\ge2\), let \(\mathcal K_n\) consist of all sets \(K=\overline\Omega\subset\mathbb C^n\), where \(\Omega\) is a nonempty bounded connected open set with \(C^\infty\) boundary.

Use the following orientation convention for pseudoconvexity. Near each \(q\in\partial K\), take a smooth real defining function \(\rho\) with \(K\cap U=\{\rho\le0\}\) and \(d\rho\ne0\) on \(\partial K\cap U\). The boundary \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex if, at every such \(q\),
\[
\sum_{j,k=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j\bar z_k}(q)v_j\overline{v_k}\ge0
\qquad\text{whenever}\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{n}\rho_{z_j}(q)v_j=0.
\]

An open set \(Y\subset\mathbb C^n\) is called Oka if, for every integer \(m\ge1\), every nonempty compact convex set \(Q\subset\mathbb C^m\), every holomorphic map \(f:V\to Y\) on an open neighbourhood \(V\) of \(Q\), and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there is a holomorphic map \(F:\mathbb C^m\to Y\) satisfying
\[
\sup_{x\in Q}\|F(x)-f(x)\|<\varepsilon,
\]
where the norm is Euclidean.

Define the two sets of dimensions
\[
\begin{aligned}
S&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\bigr\},\\
N&=\bigl\{n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}:\ \text{for every }K\in\mathcal K_n,\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\text{ Oka}\ \Longrightarrow\ \partial K\text{ pseudoconvex}\bigr\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Determine exactly the ordered pair \((S,N)\).

The established complement theorem is that
\[
K\subset\mathbb C^n\ \text{compact and polynomially convex},\quad n\ge2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\ \text{is Oka}.
\]
One cannot replace “polynomially convex” here by “the closure of a smoothly bounded pseudoconvex domain” as an established general theorem. Smooth pseudoconvexity does not imply polynomial convexity; it does not even guarantee a Stein neighbourhood basis. Thus this theorem does not determine \(S\) in the question.

There is a useful necessary implication in dimension two:
\[
2\in N.
\]

\[

=\mathcal L_u(F(t);F'(t)).

Strict positivity of the Levi form on \(W\) forces \(F'=0\) there. The identity theorem makes \(F\) constant everywhere, a contradiction.

Let \(q\in\partial Y\) be a smooth strictly pseudoconvex boundary point, with local defining function \(r\), oriented so that \(Y=\{r<0\}\).

\[

\[

\[

\phi\le-\epsilon R^2
\quad\text{on }Y\cap\partial B(q,R).

\[
u(z)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{\phi(z),c\},&z\in Y\cap B(q,R),\\
c,&z\in Y\setminus B(q,R).
\end{cases}

The missing analytic input is the **Oka complement theorem for \(q\)-complete domains**, in the following form:

> If \(D\Subset\mathbb C^n\) has smooth boundary and is \(q\)-complete for some \(q<n\), then \(\mathbb C^n\setminus\overline D\) is Oka.
>
> Here \(q\)-complete means that \(D\) has a smooth proper exhaustion whose Levi form has at least \(n-q+1\) positive eigenvalues everywhere.

The conclusion is the Oka property, hence precisely the convex approximation property used in the question. Importantly, the theorem does **not** require polynomial convexity of \(\overline D\), or a Stein neighbourhood basis.

With this input, the answer is
\[
\boxed{(S,N)=\bigl(\mathbb Z_{\ge2},\{2\}\bigr).}
\]

### 1. Every dimension belongs to \(S\)

Suppose \(K=\overline\Omega\in\mathcal K_n\) and \(\partial K\) is pseudoconvex with the stated orientation. The Levi problem implies that \(\Omega\) is Stein, and therefore \(1\)-complete.

Since \(1<n\), the complement theorem gives
\[
\mathbb C^n\setminus K\quad\text{Oka}.
\]
Thus \(S=\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).

### 2. Dimension two belongs to \(N\)

An Oka domain cannot have a smooth strongly pseudoconvex boundary point, oriented toward that domain.

Indeed, at such a point \(q\), take a defining function \(r<0\) on the domain. For sufficiently large \(A\),
\[
R=r+Ar^2
\]
is strictly plurisubharmonic near \(q\). Subtracting a sufficiently small multiple of \(\|z-q\|^2\), and then taking the maximum with a negative constant, produces a bounded continuous plurisubharmonic function on the whole domain that is strictly plurisubharmonic on a nonempty open cap near \(q\).

Let n>=2, K be a compact smooth domain, and suppose its outward Levi form has at least one positive complex-tangent direction at every boundary point. Then every continuous bounded-above plurisubharmonic function on Y=C^n minus K is constant, provided Y is connected.

1. Exterior of a Euclidean ball is scalar-Liouville. Through any p outside the ball, the affine complex lines in directions v near a Hermitian-orthogonal direction to p miss the ball. Choose n complex-linearly independent such directions; they remain safe through all points in a small neighborhood of p. Bounded subharmonic Liouville on each whole line makes u invariant under sufficiently small translations in each of these directions. Thus u is locally constant, and the exterior of the ball is connected.

2. Let u be continuous bounded-above psh on Y. By (1), u=c outside a sufficiently large ball containing K. If u is nonconstant, the maximum principle says it never attains its supremum M, so M>c. A maximizing sequence has a subsequence tending to a point q of boundary K; an interior limit would attain M.

3. Let p_j be that subsequence, q_j its nearest boundary point. Write p_j=q_j+t_j N_j, where t_j>0 tends to0, and choose smoothly varying complex normal vectors with partial rho(q_j)N_j=1.
